title: Customer-managed edge handshake proposal (WIP)
content:
Purpose and scope:

This note captures a lightweight PRD sketch for a Customer-Managed Edge Handshake: a reproducible, auditable onboarding and approval flow for private deployments where customers manage part of the network (VPCs, edge gateways, transit routers). The goal is to combine (a) an explicit approval gate model that surfaces operator intent, (b) an immutable audit trail suitable for SOC/ISO reviews, and (c) an automated handshake protocol that reduces manual steps while preserving the customer’s network ownership.

Why this exists (short):
- Many Private customers request control of networking but still need Redwood to perform runtime operations (service registration, egress routing, metric scraping, log export).
- Current handovers are ad-hoc (email + zipped configs). That causes slow onboarding and audit gaps.
- We need a pattern that satisfies compliance (immutable logs + clear approver provenance) but doesn’t require full ticket overhead for every minor change.

Key principles:
- Minimal blast radius: default to read-only or ephemeral access until explicit approval.
- Mutual attestation: both Redwood operator and customer designate an approving identity (person or service principal) and sign the handshake.
- Audit-first: every step generates an append-only event captured in both Redwood logs and optionally exported to a customer-controlled S3/GCS for long-term retention.
- Rollbackable: if handshake fails or is revoked, all pointers and credentials are automatically rotated and stale routes disabled.

Core components (proposed):
1) Edge Handshake API (server): endpoints to propose, approve, audit, revoke.
   - POST /handshakes - create proposal (includes CIDR, edge-ip, expected routes, certificate fingerprint, requested scopes)
   - GET /handshakes/{id} - read state and event stream (immutable event ids)
   - POST /handshakes/{id}/approve - customer or Redwood approver signs with short-lived attestation token
   - POST /handshakes/{id}/revoke - trigger rollback runbook

2) Approval gates and roles:
   - Gate types: network-approval (customer), ops-approval (Redwood), compliance-approval (optional).
   - Approvers: identity must be either a named Redwood employee (SSO) or a customer admin listed in onboarding manifest.
   - Approvals use short-lived cryptographic tokens (OIDC/MTLS) and are captured as part of the event.

3) Audit log model (append-only):
   - Event fields (text example): event_id | timestamp | actor | actor_type | action | subject | metadata_hash | previous_event_id | signature_id
   - Events are written to: (a) Redwood immutable store (30-90 day retention by default), (b) optional push to customer S3/GCS (customer retention policy).
   - Logs are-exportable in NDJSON for forensic review.

4) Networking artifacts and ownership:
   - Customer supplies network manifest: allowed CIDRs, NAT/eip expectations, expected peering ASNs, firewall rules.
   - Redwood produces a derived config and a deterministic config-hash. Both sides use this hash in the handshake to avoid drift.

5) Minimal UI flows (Console):
   - Onboard flow: Upload manifest -> Redwood generates proposal -> Customer reviews -> Customer approves -> Redwood accepts -> automation runs.
   - Approver UI shows diffs between proposed and current configs, highlights high-risk changes (new public egress, wide CIDRs, open 0.0.0.0/0 ingress).

6) Rollout / automatic fallback:
   - Canary mode: apply new handshake to a single operator pool for 24h, observe metrics (latency, connection errors), then promote.
   - If monitoring detects failure or the customer revokes, run automated rollback: withdraw routes, rotate any credentials, mark handshake as revoked in event stream.

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- API allows proposals and approvals, and records events to Redwood store.
- Console exposes the approval gate with clear approver identities and timestamps.
- Audit export to customer S3 works end-to-end (configurable bucket + credentials).
- Handshake revocation triggers a safe rollback path and posts events.
- Default retention / SLOs documented for audit events (e.g., 90 days hot, 1 year archive optional).

Operational and security considerations:
- Key management: handshake tokens signed via Redwood KMS. For high-security customers offer HSM-backed signing (customer-provided HSM integration as opt-in).
- Least privilege: any automation that modifies customer routing should run under a scoped service-account with TTL.
- Tamper-evidence: events include content-hash and signature; changes to the event log trigger an alert.
- Privacy: don't include raw secret material in logs. Store only fingerprints and references.
- Legal: propose an onboarding addendum clarifying that the audit export destination is customer-controlled and Redwood will only push events when explicitly instructed.

Telemetry / SLOs / Observability:
- Metrics to capture: handshake-created-rate, approval-latency-p50/p90, handshake-failure-rate, rollback-duration, events-export-latency.
- Alerting: handshake-failure-rate > 2% for more than 30m, export-failure > 5 failed attempts, and approval-stuck > 48 hours.
- Correlate handshake events with infra metrics (connection failures, abnormal TLS renegotiation counts).

Migration / roll-forward plan (phased):
- Phase 0: manual pilot with 2 customers, run CLI scripts that create events and write to Redwood store. Collect feedback. (2-4 weeks)
- Phase 1: edge-handshake API + console; support S3 export and basic rollback automation. (6-8 weeks)
- Phase 2: HSM + advanced compliance features (signing with customer HSM, SOC export format), retention policy UI. (quarterly)

Open questions / decisions to make:
- Retention defaults: 90 days vs 180 days for Redwood hot store? (legal and infra cost tradeoffs)
- Should approvals support delegated approvals (group-based) or strictly individual signatures?
- Export formats for customers who want SIEM ingestion (CEF vs NDJSON vs Syslog).
- Legal: what liability language do we need for automated rollback affecting customer runtime?
- Do we allow Redwood to auto-approve low-risk diffs when a customer made a policy-level allow earlier? (saved time vs safety)

Quick TODOs / next steps:
- [ ] Align with Security on event schema and signature model (owners: Ben + Priya)
- [ ] Spike: simple CLI that writes a signed event to store and pushes to a GCS bucket (owner: Kyle)
- [ ] Draft onboarding addendum for Legal review (owner: Mariana)
- [ ] Design console wireframe for approval diff view (owner: Product-UX)
- [ ] Create JIRA epic and sub-tasks (PD-4321 exists; expand)

Notes / context snippets from earlier threads:
- "Customer wants control but still needs Redwood metrics" — thread in #private-deploy-prodops, Jan 14 2026.
- Confluence draft PD-1234 contains full event field list and sample export consumer configs.

Appendix: example event (human-readable, single line)
- 2026-03-05T18:12:49Z | e1a7f3 | Aisha Kapoor (redwood:operator) | create_proposal | subject:edge-handshake:cmp-42 | config_hash:sha256:abcd... | signature:rk-9001

Rough UX notes:
- Show a clear label when the customer is expected to approve (email + in-console notification).
- Allow approver to 'request changes' with a mandatory comment that becomes part of the log.
- Provide 'reason codes' for approvals (e.g., security_review_complete, operational_ready, emergency_override).

End of WIP.

If you are reviewing: add inline comments, push to PD-4321 for tracking, and flag any legal concerns in the ticket.
